title: How Resorts and Hotels Win More Direct Bookings From Google
seoTitle: How Hotels Win More Direct Bookings From Google
seoDescription: How resorts and hotels win direct bookings from Google Search and Maps instead of losing the click to online travel agencies, and how to benchmark visibility.
excerpt: When your official booking link is missing or shows the wrong price, the traveler books through an agency. Here is what decides who wins the click on Google.
imageAlt: Resort swimming pool with white umbrellas and lounge chairs under a bright blue sky
imageIdea: Real photo of a resort pool with loungers and umbrellas in daylight, inviting and bookable, no people's faces and no brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Resorts and hotels win more direct bookings from Google when their own website shows up in the same places the online travel agencies do, with a live rate, a working booking link, strong photos and steady reviews. When your official link has no price next to it, or the price does not match your booking engine, the traveler clicks the agency listing that does. That click usually costs you a commission and the guest relationship.

The good news is that Google gives independent hotels and resorts a fair way to compete for that click. Most properties are simply not set up to use it well.

Where does a hotel booking start on Google now?

For many travelers it starts with a search like a hotel name, a destination plus "resort," or a need such as "pet friendly hotel near the beach." Google answers with a hotel panel or a map of options, each with photos, a review score and a list of places to book.

That list of booking options is where direct revenue is won or lost. Your hotel can appear as its own booking choice next to the agencies. In 2022 Google said that free hotel booking links, which first launched on its travel site, would also show on the main Search results page and on Google Maps, with travelers completing the booking on the partner's own website. In other words, the same traveler who looks at your hotel on Maps can book you directly, if your link is there.

Why do online travel agencies win the click so often?

Because they show up complete. A large agency sends rates for every date, has photos for every room type and is listed in every slot Google offers. A hotel that has never connected its own rates looks like the weaker choice, even when it is the better deal.

Agencies bring guests you might not reach yourself, and most hotels need them. The problem is the guest who searched your name, was ready to book and still went through an agency because your own option was missing or looked worse. That booking should be yours.

What are free booking links, and why do they matter?

Free booking links are unpaid listings that let your own booking engine appear as an option in Google's hotel results. Google's help page on free booking links says there is no cost for clicks, that bids have no impact on how free booking links rank, and that they are ranked separately from paid hotel ads.

Booking engine providers such as Cloudbeds describe these as a link to your website's booking engine shown with an "Official Site" badge. For a traveler, that label matters. It tells them they are booking with you, not a middleman, and many guests prefer that when the price is the same.

What has to be true for your official rate to show?

Your rates have to reach Google through a connected partner, and they have to be accurate. Google ended the option to add hotel rates by hand through the Business Profile on July 30, 2025, according to its rates and availability FAQ. Google's connectivity partner guide explains that the partner can be a central reservation system, an internet booking engine, a channel manager or a property management system.

Accuracy is not optional. Google's price accuracy policy says the total price on your booking page should match the total shown on Google, mandatory taxes and fees must be disclosed, and the price must match the dates and number of guests the traveler chose. Google also says itineraries with inaccurate prices may not be shown at all.

What Google needsWhat good looks like
A connected rate feedYour booking engine or reservation system is connected to Google and sending live rates and availability
Prices that matchThe total a guest sees on Google is the total they see on your booking page, including resort fees and taxes
The right dates and guestsYour booking page opens on the dates and occupancy the guest picked, not your home page
A link to your own siteThe website and booking links on your profile point to your domain, not an agency or a social page

Resort fees deserve special attention. If the fee appears only at the last step, the price on Google and the price at checkout will not agree, and you risk both the listing and the guest's trust.

Do photos and reviews still decide the click?

Yes. A live rate gets you into the comparison, but photos and reviews decide whether the traveler picks you. Google's guide on how to improve local ranking says review count and review score factor into local ranking, and that there is no way to pay for a better local position.

Think about what a resort guest is really buying: the pool, the room view, the spa, the beach access. If your Google photos are old, dark or mostly uploaded by guests at odd angles, the agency listing with polished photos of the same property can look like the better place to book. Your Google profile should show the experience you sell, room by room and amenity by amenity, and it should be refreshed when anything changes.

How do you know if you are getting your fair share of visibility?

Benchmark yourself against a comp set, the handful of properties a guest would realistically compare you with. The hotel industry already does this for occupancy. STR's market penetration index compares a hotel's occupancy with its competitive set and scores it so that 100 means fair share, all else being equal.

The same idea works for visibility. If you and four competitors should split the attention on the searches that matter to you, a score of 100 means you are getting your fair slice. A score of 140 means you are being seen far more than your size alone would suggest. A score of 70 means competitors, or the agencies selling your rooms, are taking attention that should be yours.

I like this framing because rankings and clicks all move with the season. A comp set score tells you whether you are gaining or losing ground against the hotels a guest is actually weighing you against.

What should a GM or revenue lead look at first?

Start by looking at your hotel the way a guest does, then ask whether each step points them to your own booking engine.

  1. Search your own name on a phone. Is your official booking option there for next weekend, and does it show a price?
  2. Compare your price with what you see on your site. If they differ, find out why before you do anything else.
  3. Look at your photos as a stranger would. Would they sell the stay better than the agency listing does?
  4. Read your last 20 reviews and replies. Recent, answered reviews are part of the decision.
  5. Pick your comp set. Decide which four to six properties a guest really compares you with, and measure against them over time.

This is the work we do for resorts, hotels and boutique stays at The SocialDM, across Google Search, Google Maps and AI answers. You can see how it fits together on our hospitality marketing page. Rate strategy and distribution stay with your revenue team. Our job is to make sure that when a guest is ready to book, your own option is visible, accurate and the easiest one to choose.

Questions we hear

Why does Google show online travel agencies above my hotel's own website?

Often because the agencies are sending live rates for your dates and your own site is not. A traveler comparing prices on Google clicks the option that shows a price. Getting your own rate to show, accurately, is the first step to winning that click back.

Do free booking links cost anything?

Google says there is no cost for clicks on free booking links, and that bids have no impact on how free booking links are ranked. They are ranked separately from paid hotel ads.

Can I still type my rates into my Google Business Profile?

No. Google ended adding hotel rates through the Business Profile on July 30, 2025. To show rates now, a hotel works with a connected partner such as its booking engine, central reservation system, channel manager or property management system.

What does a visibility score of 100 against a comp set mean?

It means you are getting exactly your fair share compared with the hotels you compete with. Above 100 means you are capturing more than your share, below 100 means less. It borrows the logic of the hotel industry's occupancy index.

Can a hotel pay Google to rank higher on Maps or in free booking links?

No. Google says there is no way to pay for a better local ranking, and bids do not affect free booking link ranking. Paid hotel ads are a separate product.

No cost for clicks on free booking links; bids have no impact on free booking link ranking; free links are ranked separately from ads
Free booking links show a link to the hotel's own booking engine with an Official Site badge
Adding hotel rates through Google Business Profile ended July 30, 2025; hotels should work with a partner to keep rates visible
Connectivity partners can be a central reservation system, internet booking engine, channel manager or property management system
Total price on the booking page should match Google; mandatory taxes and fees must be disclosed; price must match selected dates and occupancy; inaccurate itineraries may not be shown
Review count and score factor into local ranking; no way to pay for a better local ranking

takeaways: Travelers often book through an agency simply because your own booking option on Google is missing or shows no price.
Google says free booking links cost nothing per click and bids do not affect how they rank.
Since July 30, 2025, hotel rates reach Google through a connected partner, not by typing them into the Business Profile.
Google's price accuracy policy expects the total on your booking page, including mandatory fees, to match what Google shows.
Benchmark visibility against a comp set, where 100 means fair share, to see whether you are gaining or losing ground.
